standard.title: Analyse Cause and Effect, Evaluate Continuity and Change
standard.description: analyse cause and effect and evaluate patterns of continuity and change
standard.prior_knowledge: In Year 7 students described causes and effects and explained continuities and changes (AC9HH7S05). In Year 8 they continued with description and explanation (AC9HH8S05). Y9 lifts the demand — from describe/explain to analyse cause-and-effect and evaluate continuity/change patterns. The addition of 'evaluate' signals that students must now make judgements about significance, not only describe relationships.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse cause and effect and evaluate patterns of continuity and change across the topics being studied.

nodes.label: Analysing cause-and-effect relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse cause-and-effect relationships in historical events, distinguishing between long-term, medium-term and immediate causes, and explaining how causes are interconnected.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least two causes of one historical event, explaining the relationship between them.
nodes.typical_width: Create a timeline identifying significant events or individuals across a period; analyse cause-and-effect patterns including distinguishing between long-term structural causes and immediate triggers; explain how multiple causes interact (e.g. MAIN causes of WWI plus the assassination as trigger); organise primary sources and perspectives chronologically to support historical argument.
wider: Construct a multi-causal analysis of a complex historical event (e.g. the outbreak of WWI or the Industrial Revolution) using a structured framework distinguishing long-term, medium-term and immediate causes — applying the skill at its most demanding level
Apply cause-and-effect analysis to two contrasting historical events in the same unit to demonstrate the skill's transferability
Use quantitative data sources (e.g. population records, casualty figures) alongside qualitative sources to build a cause-and-effect argument — practising the integration of different evidence types

response_modes.reason: The distinction between long-term structural causes and immediate triggers is the key analytical move at Year 9. Students who only identify immediate causes cannot analyse historical causation at the expected depth — explicit scaffolding of the long/short-term distinction is necessary.

success_criteria: Identifies and analyses at least three causes of one historical event, distinguishing between long-term and immediate causes
Explains how at least two causes are connected — demonstrating causal complexity rather than parallel listing

nodes.label: Evaluating patterns of continuity and change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate patterns of continuity and change across a period, making judgements about the significance of changes and the persistence of continuities.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one significant pattern of change and one continuity across a period being studied, explaining why each is significant.
nodes.typical_width: Organise primary sources and perspectives chronologically to support historical argument about continuities and changes; evaluate whether changes were rapid or gradual, widespread or limited, reversible or permanent; assess which continuities were most significant and which changes had the greatest long-term impact.
wider: Apply continuity and change analysis to two different social groups experiencing the same historical period (e.g. colonisers and colonised) — examining how the same period produced different patterns for different groups

Evaluate continuity and change across three different domains (social, political, economic) for the same period — assessing whether change was more or less rapid in different domains and explaining why

Construct a historical argument about whether a particular period (e.g. Federation, the Industrial Revolution) represented genuine transformation or primarily continuity — supporting the argument with evidence from multiple source types

response_modes.reason: Applying the continuity/change framework to multiple groups, multiple domains, or multiple topics builds the skill as a genuine analytical capacity rather than a template applied once.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evaluating continuity and change patterns across different groups and domains is the most powerful application of this skill — it reveals how historical change is uneven, contested, and experienced differently depending on social position.
success_criteria: Evaluates at least one pattern of change and one continuity, making a judgement about the significance of each
Explains why at least one change was significant or why one continuity persisted, with reference to historical evidence
